questions.question: Translational equilibrium requires that the
options: net external torque about one point is zero
normal force always equals the weight
static friction must be at its maximum value
questions.explanation: Translational equilibrium requires the net external force to be zero (ΣF = 0). Torque concerns rotational equilibrium; normal force need not equal weight; friction need not be maximum.

questions.question: Rotational equilibrium requires that the
options: angular momentum must always be zero
net external torque about any point is zero
all forces must pass through the centre of mass
questions.explanation: Rotational equilibrium requires the net external torque about any point to be zero (Στ = 0). Angular momentum need only be constant, not zero.

questions.question: A body moving with constant velocity is in
questions.explanation: A body with constant velocity has zero acceleration and hence zero net force, so it is in dynamic translational equilibrium.

questions.question: If the net external force on a body is zero, its centre of mass
questions.explanation: By Newton's second law for the system, zero net force gives zero acceleration of the centre of mass, so it moves with constant velocity (possibly zero).

questions.question: A body may have zero net force but still not be in mechanical equilibrium if
questions.explanation: Mechanical equilibrium requires both ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0. If the net torque is nonzero, the body will rotationally accelerate and is not in equilibrium.

questions.question: A couple produces
options: pure torque with zero net force
zero torque but nonzero net force
no rotational tendency because forces cancel
questions.explanation: A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces. It produces pure torque with zero net force, so it causes rotation but not translation.

questions.question: Torque is defined as the
options: dot product of force and displacement
ratio of force to moment arm
questions.explanation: Torque is the vector τ = r × F, where r is the position vector from the pivot to the point of application and F is the force.

questions.question: The moment arm of a force is the
options: distance from pivot to point of application
perpendicular distance to line of action
length of the force vector itself
angle between position vector and force
questions.explanation: The moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. Torque magnitude = force × moment arm.

questions.question: The SI unit of torque is
questions.explanation: Torque has units of force × distance, so the SI unit is the newton metre (N m).

questions.question: The principle of moments states that for rotational equilibrium
options: all forces must have equal magnitudes
the centre of gravity must lie at the pivot
total torque must be maximum in clockwise direction
questions.explanation: The principle of moments: for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any point.

questions.question: A force whose line of action passes through the pivot produces torque equal to
questions.explanation: If the line of action passes through the pivot, the moment arm is zero, so the torque is zero.

questions.question: A force applied at the pivot produces no torque because its
questions.explanation: A force applied at the pivot has zero moment arm, so torque = force × 0 = 0.

questions.question: To find unknown forces in a static rigid body, one uses
questions.explanation: In general, a rigid body has unknown forces and their lines of action, so both force equilibrium (ΣF = 0) and torque equilibrium (Στ = 0) are needed.

questions.question: A free-body diagram shows
options: all external forces acting on the body
only forces exerted by the body
only the net force and net torque
internal forces between particles of the body
questions.explanation: A free-body diagram shows all external forces acting on the body. Internal forces cancel and are not shown.

questions.question: For three coplanar forces in equilibrium, the force vectors
options: all point in the same direction
form an open polygon with no resultant
questions.explanation: Three coplanar forces in equilibrium have a vector sum of zero, so they form a closed triangle (triangle of forces).

questions.question: For a picture frame suspended symmetrically by two equal tensions, the horizontal components of tension
options: vanish only if the angle is zero
questions.explanation: In a symmetric suspension, the two horizontal components are equal and opposite, so they cancel each other. Only the vertical components add to balance the weight.

questions.question: A box sliding down a ramp at constant velocity has net force along the incline equal to
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force along the incline is zero: the weight component down the slope is exactly balanced by kinetic friction up the slope.

questions.question: Friction
options: acts only when object is moving
is always larger than any applied horizontal force
questions.explanation: Friction is the force that opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion between surfaces in contact.

questions.question: While an object remains at rest under a horizontal push, static friction is
options: completely independent of the applied horizontal force
questions.explanation: While the object is at rest, static friction adjusts to be equal and opposite to the applied force, up to a maximum value. It is not necessarily at its maximum.

questions.question: Maximum static friction occurs
options: only when normal force is zero
only when object is in neutral equilibrium
questions.explanation: Static friction increases with the applied force until it reaches its maximum just before sliding begins; at that point μsN is fully mobilised.

questions.question: The coefficient of static friction is generally
questions.explanation: For most surfaces, μs > μk: it takes more force to start motion than to maintain it. So the coefficient of static friction is generally greater.

questions.question: Friction is independent of the
questions.explanation: For a given pair of surfaces and a given normal force, kinetic friction is approximately independent of the apparent area of contact (a consequence of the way real contact area scales with normal force).

questions.question: Kinetic friction is independent of the
questions.explanation: Kinetic friction is approximately independent of the speed of the object over a wide range (though it does depend on the normal force, nature of surfaces, and μk).

questions.question: If the applied force exceeds maximum static friction, the object
questions.explanation: Once the applied force exceeds the maximum static friction, the object begins to slide; kinetic friction then acts.

questions.question: A smooth frictionless wall means
options: friction at base must be zero
questions.explanation: A smooth frictionless wall means there is no friction at the wall; only a normal force acts from the wall.

questions.question: In stable equilibrium, after a small displacement the centre of gravity
questions.explanation: In stable equilibrium, a small displacement causes the centre of gravity to rise, so gravity provides a restoring torque that returns the body.

questions.question: In unstable equilibrium, after a small displacement the centre of gravity
questions.explanation: In unstable equilibrium, a small displacement causes the centre of gravity to lower, so gravity pulls the body further away.

questions.question: In neutral equilibrium, after a small displacement the centre of gravity
questions.explanation: In neutral equilibrium, a small displacement leaves the centre of gravity at the same level, so there is no restoring or disturbing torque.

questions.question: Stable equilibrium is typically associated with
questions.explanation: Stability is promoted by a low centre of gravity and a wide base, which make it harder to tip the body over.

questions.question: A cone lying on its side is an example of
questions.explanation: A cone lying on its side can roll without changing the height of its centre of gravity, so it is in neutral equilibrium.

questions.question: A cone balanced on its tip is an example of
questions.explanation: A cone on its tip has its centre of gravity at its highest point; any small displacement lowers it and topples the cone, so it is in unstable equilibrium.

questions.question: For rotational equilibrium in two dimensions, about any point the
options: only moments about centre of mass count
net force must also be maximum
questions.explanation: For rotational equilibrium, the sum of moments (torques) about any point is zero. The choice of point is arbitrary, not restricted to the centre of mass.
